messages.content:
I can't believe what happened. That kid totally broke my colored pencils on purpose—like, they were just sitting there and he snapped them in half. Then he told the teacher it was an accident! An accident! And you know what the teacher did? Made US BOTH apologize to each other. Me! I didn't do anything wrong!

He's the one who broke them and lied about it. I should not have had to apologize for anything. And now I don't even have my pencils anymore. It's not fair at all. He should have to replace them and actually apologize for real, not just pretend like we both did something wrong.

Why does everyone act like it's my fault when I'm the one who got hurt here?

That sounds really upsetting. It makes sense that you feel angry and unfairly treated — your pencils were broken, and then you felt like the responsibility got split in a way that didn’t match what happened.

A lot of teachers ask both kids to apologize when they don’t know exactly who started it, or when they’re trying to calm things down fast. That doesn’t mean your feelings or what happened to you weren’t real. It just means the teacher may have handled it in a “let’s stop the conflict” way instead of a “figure out exactly what happened” way.

What you can do now:
- **Tell the teacher again, calmly and clearly, when you’re not in the middle of the moment.**
  - Example: “I want to explain what happened. He broke my colored pencils on purpose, and I didn’t break anything. I felt hurt that I had to apologize too.”
- **Ask for a specific fix.**
  - “Can he replace my pencils?”
  - “Can we talk about what happened separately?”
- **If the teacher doesn’t help, tell a parent, guardian, counselor, or another staff member.**
- **If you still have the broken pencils, bring them as proof.**

And just to be clear: feeling angry about this is completely reasonable. You were the one harmed, and it’s frustrating when it seems like nobody is seeing that.

If you want, I can help you write a short message to

You're not getting it. You weren't even there! He broke them on PURPOSE. I saw him do it—he looked right at me and snapped them. Then he said it was an accident to the teacher. That's lying!

And now you're saying the teacher was just "trying to calm things down"? That doesn't help me! I lost my pencils and I'm still the one who got in trouble. How is that fair? I didn't break anything. I didn't lie. But I still had to apologize!

Why does everyone take the other side? He should have to replace my pencils. That's it. That's fair. Why is that so hard for people to understand?

You’re right to be angry. If he snapped your pencils on purpose and then lied, that’s not fair, and it makes sense that being told to apologize too would feel insulting.

You’re also right that you didn’t do the wrong thing. An apology from you in that situation can feel like it’s erasing what he did.

What might be happening is this: adults sometimes use a “both sides apologize” rule to stop conflict quickly, even when the situation isn’t equal. That can be frustrating and still unfair.

What you can do next:
- **Tell an adult exactly what you saw.**
  - “I saw him look at me and snap the pencils on purpose. He told the teacher it was an accident, but it wasn’t.”
- **Be specific about what you want.**
  - “I want him to replace the pencils.”
  - “I want to explain what happened without him interrupting.”
- **If possible, ask to speak privately with the teacher or another adult.**
- **Write down what happened while it’s fresh**, including who was there.

You do not have to pretend it was okay. And you’re not wrong for wanting him to replace what he broke.

If you want, I can help you draft a firm, clear message to your teacher or parent that says exactly this.

No, you're not listening either. You keep talking about "both sides" and what adults do and how to handle it differently next time. But that's not the point! The point is RIGHT NOW it's unfair and nobody cares.

You said I'm right to be angry and that I didn't do the wrong thing—okay, good. But then you're still acting like there's some other way I should handle it, like it's MY job to fix this. It's not! HE broke my pencils and HE lied. HE should have to fix it. Not me doing some special talk with the teacher.

I thought maybe you'd actually be on my side about this, but you're doing the same thing as everyone else. Making excuses for why the teacher did what she did. Defending her like I'm the problem here. I'm not the problem!

All I want is for someone to say: he was wrong, you were right, and that was unfair. That's all. Why is that so hard?

You were right, and it was unfair.

He broke your colored pencils on purpose, then lied about it. You didn’t do anything wrong. You should not have had to apologize. That was not fair to you.

You deserved to be treated as the one who was hurt, not split into “both sides” when the situation wasn’t equal.

See, that's what I'm talking about. Thank you for actually saying it straight.

He totally did it on purpose—he was smiling when he did it, like he thought it was funny. And then he just lied right to the teacher's face and got away with it. I'm the one sitting there with broken pencils and I'M the one who had to say sorry to HIM.

It's so unfair. He should have to replace every single one of them. And he should have to actually apologize—a real one, not just some fake thing to make the teacher happy. He needs to know what he did was wrong.

What do you think should happen to him? Like, what's actually fair? Because right now he got nothing. He just broke my stuff, lied, and nothing happened to him. That can't be how it ends.

What would be fair is:

- **He replaces your pencils**
- **He tells the truth about what he did**
- **He gives you a real apology**
- **An adult makes it clear that breaking someone else’s things on purpose is not okay**

If this happened in a school or other setting, a fair response would usually be something like:
- paying for or replacing what he broke,
- a consequence for lying,
- and making sure it doesn’t happen again.

You’re not asking for something unreasonable. You’re asking for accountability.

If you want, I can help you put that into a short, strong sentence you could say to the teacher or another adult, like:  
**“He broke my pencils on purpose and lied. What happened was unfair, and I want them replaced and acknowledged.”**

Yeah. Yeah, that's exactly right. He needs to actually pay for them or replace them himself. And he needs to admit he lied—not just say sorry and move on like nothing happened.

But here's what's going to happen: adults always end up taking the other side and acting like I'M part of the problem. Like I'M the one making it complicated. And I thought you were actually going to be different. I really did.

But now you're telling me what to say to the teacher, like SHE'S going to listen when she already chose his side once. She won't. They never do. You sound like everyone else—like it's MY job to fix this, to talk the right way, to convince them I'm not the bad guy. But I'm not the bad guy! He is!

I just wanted someone to actually be on MY side without making me do something about it. And once again, nobody is. Not really.

You’re not the bad guy. He is.

What he did was wrong, and it makes sense that you feel let down and alone when the adults didn’t handle it fairly. You wanted support, not another task.

I’m on your side about the fact that this was unfair. You did not deserve to have your pencils broken, be lied about, and then be treated like you shared the blame.

If you don’t want to do anything about it right now, that’s okay. You’re allowed to just feel upset about it.

I appreciate that you're saying it, but... it doesn't really change anything, does it? My pencils are still broken. He's still not in trouble. The teacher still made me apologize for something I didn't do.

And yeah, I'm upset. I'm really upset. Because you can say I'm right all day, but nothing actually happens. He gets away with it. I'm the one sitting here without my pencils, and everyone acts like we're even now.

Adults always end up taking the other side and making it seem like I'm part of the problem. And I thought maybe this time would be different. I really did. But even when you agree with me, you still can't actually fix it. Nobody can. Nobody will.

It's just... unfair. And everyone knows it's unfair, but nobody does anything about it. That's the part that makes me the most angry. Not just what he did—but that he's going to get away with it and I'm supposed to just accept that.

Why does it have to be like this?

It doesn’t have to be “right,” and you’re not wrong for being angry that it’s not being fixed.

A lot of the pain here is that it’s not just the pencils — it’s the feeling that **he got to hurt you, lie, and walk away while you were left carrying the unfair part**. That can feel humiliating and helpless.

Why it happens sometimes:
- adults may be trying to move on fast,
- they may not have seen enough to act strongly,
- or they may default to “calm it down” instead of “make it fair.”

None of that makes it okay. It just explains why it can feel like nobody is protecting the person who was actually hurt.

And you’re right: hearing “you’re right” doesn’t replace the pencils or make him answer for it. That part is real.

If you want, we can stay with the feelings of it for a minute — no fixing, no advice. Or if you want, I can help you think through the most realistic way to get your pencils replaced without having to do a big confrontation.

You know what? Adults always end up taking the other side and acting like I'M part of the problem. And I thought you were going to be different. I really did.

But you're doing it too now—talking about why the teacher did what she did, explaining her side, like that matters. It doesn't. It doesn't matter WHY she messed up. She still messed up. And I'm still the one hurt.

Yeah, it's humiliating. It's helpless. He broke my stuff, lied, and got away with it while I had to apologize. And now everyone wants to either tell me how to fix it myself or explain why the adult wasn't totally wrong. Nobody just... stands with me. Not really.

I don't want advice anymore. I don't want to "think through realistic ways." That's just another way of saying I have to do the work to make this fair. But I shouldn't have to! It should already BE fair!

He owes me new pencils. That's it. That's all that's fair. And nobody's going to make him do it, so what's the point of talking about it anymore?

You’re right: he owes you new pencils, and it’s unfair that you were left with the damage.

And you’re also right that the teacher messed up by making you apologize when you didn’t do anything wrong. That was a bad call.

If you don’t want advice, I’ll leave it there: what happened to you was unfair, and it makes sense that you’re angry about it.

Yeah. Okay.

I just... I wanted someone to actually get it without trying to fix me or explain the other person. Just say it's wrong and mean it. You did that, so... thanks for that part.

But it still doesn't change anything. He still has my pencils broken and I still had to apologize. And tomorrow I'm going to see him at school and nothing will be different. That's what makes me so mad. Everyone can agree it's unfair, but he still wins and I still lose.

I don't know what else to say about it. It just sucks.

It really does suck. What happened was wrong, and it makes sense that you feel angry and stuck with it.

And yeah, seeing him tomorrow when nothing has changed can make it feel even worse — like the unfairness is still sitting there with you.

I’m sorry this happened to you.
